job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Yusuf Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent: no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My day starts at seven with coffee and the train into town. At Calder Insurance Brokers I'm a sales support analyst, which means preparing quotes, checking policy documents and answering account managers' questions. I did a business degree and passed, with no internships. I rent a room in a shared flat, and on Saturdays I go to Calder Bay to help my father at his hardware shop, where I do the stock sheets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's a relief for people who were scared, and a lesson about believing every sales pitch. At work I'd tell my colleagues the firm can keep working the way it works. With my brothers at the weekend I'd joke that Dad's old ledger beat all the apps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be content. I'm a sales support analyst at Calder Insurance Brokers, preparing quotes and checking policy documents for the account managers. I use an AI tool now and then to tidy up a draft, and it's fine. I like that my job doesn't feel at risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the quotes and policy checks, and take the insurance exams the firm sponsors, one paper every six months. I'd pay 200 a month on my loan and save 120. On Saturdays I'd keep helping Dad at his hardware shop in Calder Bay, where I do the stock sheets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. I'd feel settled and a bit proud that I'm earning my own way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the takings at your dad's shop. What do you see in the book?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What I'd worry about is the shop. Dad is 58, and a big chain opened ten minutes away last year. He says nothing, but I see the takings in the book. That has nothing to do with AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does looking after your family mean in practice for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the shop went under, I'd want to be in a position to help him. That's partly why I'm saving. A man should look after his family, and I'd say that to anyone.

say: I'd say it's a **relief** for people who were scared, and a lesson about sales pitches.
I'd joke that Dad's old **ledger** beat all the apps.
think: I'd be **content**, since my job doesn't feel at risk.
The real worry is my dad's **hardware shop** losing customers to a chain.
do: Take one **insurance exam** paper every six months, sponsored by the firm.
Pay **200 a month** on the loan and save 120.
Keep doing the **stock sheets** at Dad's shop on Saturdays.
feel: I'd feel **good**, settled and a bit proud to earn my own way.
S0.quote: A man should look after his family, and I'd say that to anyone.
fieldNote: Yusuf is **content** at work, but his family's shop and a nearby chain are the real weight on him.
His saving is partly a **duty** to his father, which comes from a traditional view of family.

steps.text: Sit one insurance exam paper every six months
Pay 200 a month on the loan and save 120
Do the stock sheets at Dad's shop on Saturdays

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's not be afraid of it, we should use it and keep our standards. At work I'd offer to try the tools before the bosses decide for us. With family I'd say a business that doesn't adapt closes, and that's just how it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, quotes, policy checks and answering customers are what it takes first. My job is mostly that, and a broker with software might do it with half the support staff. But I use the tools now and then, so I'm not starting from zero.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my manager, Rohan, to put me on whatever pilot the firm runs, so I'm the one who knows the system. I'd work on getting my licence as a broker, which is the human, selling side, within a year. And I'd put 250 a month away instead of 120.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm a little uneasy. I trust the market to sort it out in the long run, but I'm not sure about the first two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why is the broker licence more human work, in your eyes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would say he never needed a degree to run a shop, and that's partly true. But he'd also want me to stay in a proper office job. I'd tell him I'm planning for both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would an online ordering system change for your dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also start telling Dad to try a basic online ordering system at the shop, because that's one thing I could do. If the shop gets its stock automatically, we save time. It also gives me a way to be useful to the family.

say: I'd say let's not be afraid, we should **use it** and keep our standards.
I'd say a business that doesn't **adapt** closes.
think: Quotes, policy checks and answering customers are what it takes **first**, and that's most of my job.
I trust the market in the long run, but not the **first two years**.
do: Ask Rohan to put me on the firm's **pilot**.
Get my **broker licence** within a year.
Put **250 a month** away instead of 120.
feel: I'd feel a bit **uneasy** about the first two years.

fieldNote: Yusuf takes the **market view** that firms adapt, but he sees the first two years as the risky stretch.
He plans to cover **both** the firm and his father's shop, using his tool skills for each.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is too short, and our leaders are not honest about what's coming. At work I'd ask for a straight plan. With family I'd say we'll stick together, because that's what families do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job goes by 2028, along with most desk jobs. The firm will hold on to a few brokers who have the client relationships. A support analyst won't be one of them. I'm scared of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut every cost, move back to my parents' house to save the 480 rent, and put 400 a month away. I'd work full-time with Dad at the shop, starting with putting stock and ordering online. Hands-on work in a shop gets about three more years. I'd also try to become the first person in the family to run two businesses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a bit determined as well. I know what I'd do, and that helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your father the night you decided to go full-time at the shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father would be proud and also upset that his son's degree didn't help. I'd tell him it isn't wasted. I'd say I need him to teach me what he knows, because someday I'll run the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't wait for the government. Why not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The one thing I wouldn't do is wait for the government. Help can come, and I'd take it, but I'd rather build something with my family and neighbours. Customers who know your name stay with you, and that's all I'd have.

say: I'd say two years is **too short**, and leaders aren't honest about what's coming.
think: My job goes by **2028**, because a support analyst won't be among the few brokers kept.
I know what I'd do, and that **helps**.
do: Move back to my **parents' house** to save the 480 rent.
Put **400 a month** away and go full-time at Dad's shop.
Move the shop's stock and ordering **online**.
feel: I'd be **anxious**, but a bit determined.
S2.quote: Customers who know your name stay with you, and that's all I'd have.
fieldNote: Yusuf's **fallback** is the family hardware shop, where hands-on work buys about three more years.
He prefers building with **family** and neighbours to waiting for government help.

steps.text: Move back to my parents' house and save 400 a month
Go full-time at Dad's hardware shop
Put the shop's stock and ordering online
Ask Dad to teach me how to run the shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time, and sensible people will use it. At work I'd say let's stay ahead of it. With family I'd say let's make a plan at Sunday lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I've got a window. If I use the next two years to build the shop and get my broker licence, I'd be fine either way. I'd still feel pressure, but it would be useful pressure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the insurance exams, get my licence, and use the tools more at work, so I'm the one who knows them. At the same time I'd put the hardware shop online, with a stock system, and run it with Dad. I'd save 300 a month and put some into the shop's setup, around 1,500.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady. Five years is long enough to make mistakes and fix them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Omar agree about the shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother Omar works at a bank, and he'd say the same, that we have time. We'd make a family agreement: if the bank job goes, he joins the shop, and I handle the office side. It's the kind of thing a family should settle before trouble starts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What signs in year two would make you leave the firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would change my plan is how fast things went in year two. If the signs were strong, I'd leave the broker's job and go full-time at the shop. I'd rather jump a year early than a year late.

At family lunch I'd say let's make a **plan**.
think: I think I've got a **window**: build the shop and get my licence, and I'd be fine either way.

Put the **hardware shop** online with a stock system, around 1,500.

feel: I'd feel **steady**: five years is long enough to make mistakes and fix them.
S3.quote: I'd rather jump a year early than a year late.
fieldNote: Yusuf treats five years as a **window** to build two paths, the licence and the family shop.
He wants a **family agreement** with his brother Omar before any trouble begins.

steps.text: Finish the insurance exams and get my broker licence
Put the hardware shop online, about 1,500

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and the best thing is to build something real in the meantime. At work I'd do my job. With family I'd say that's the time to settle down and raise children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be fine. At 32 I'd have a broker's licence, maybe a share in the shop, a wife and a child. I'd be ready to change if something clearly proved to be better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at the firm for four or five years, get my licence and then decide. I'd buy a small flat by 28 with about 15,000 saved. I'd marry in about three years, and I'd keep helping Dad and bring in a stock system little by little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. It gives me room to get on with life instead of waiting for trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would marrying in three years change for your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it moved faster, I'd put the shop first and move over sooner. I'd keep it as my planned fallback. It's a good thing to have, a place that is yours and where you are known.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your younger cousins?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell younger cousins to build something that lasts: a trade, a family, a name. Titles and tools change. A good name stays.

I'd say it's the time to **settle down** and raise children.

I'd be ready to **change** if something clearly proved better.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most, because desk work like mine goes first and two years is nothing. I'd lean on the family shop. What would help is a clear plan from my firm, a fair chance to get my broker licence, and a bit of breathing room for small family shops like my father's.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: If I'm honest, I'd say I don't want a handout. I want the chance to work, build and look after my family. If the system lets me do that, I'll do the rest.

headlineQuote: I don't want a handout. I want the chance to work, build and look after my family.
portrait: Yusuf is a business graduate, four months into a sales support job at an insurance broker, **renting** a room.
He is traditional and steady: he uses AI tools now and then, trusts markets and puts family first.
His mood runs from uneasy to **anxious** as warning shortens, and his answer is always the family's hardware shop.
He prefers work and **family** support to handouts, and he is saving for a flat.
biggestWorry: The **2028** scenario worries him most, since desk work like his goes first and two years is too short.
whatWouldHelp: A clear plan from his **firm**, a fair chance at a broker licence, and breathing room for small family shops.
